notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes for Isaiah 57, drawing on the sources I was able to access.

---

## Isaiah 57 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### General Overview

The chapter falls into three main sections: (1) the blessed death of the righteous (vv. 1–2); (2) a blistering rebuke of idolatry as spiritual adultery (vv. 3–13); (3) God's promise of healing, peace, and restoration for the humble (vv. 14–21), contrasted with the restlessness of the wicked. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

Matthew Henry frames the whole as: observations on the death of good men (1–2), the gross idolatries of the Jews (3–12), and God's gracious return to restore His people (13–21). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 1 — "The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart…"

**Traditional Reading:** The verse laments that when righteous and merciful (godly) people die prematurely, the society around them shows utter indifference. No one asks what it means; no one grieves. The righteous are "taken away from the evil to come" — that is, God in His mercy removes them before impending judgment falls, so they are spared seeing or suffering it. — Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/57.htm

Calvin emphasizes that this is a providence people *should* observe: God removes the godly as a warning that calamity is near, yet the wicked take no notice. He cites the death of Luther as an example — Luther was taken shortly before the terrible war that fell on Germany, which he had foretold. — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

Ellicott places this during or anticipating Manasseh's persecution of the true prophets. The singular "righteous" points to the few conspicuous sufferers. The survivors of Hezekiah's reforms "vexed their souls even to death with the evils that were around them." — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Gill adds that "merciful men" (or "men of kindness") are those who have obtained mercy from the Lord and show mercy to others — holy, good men. They are "gathered" out of the world to escape coming evil, yet "no man lays it to heart." — Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/57.htm

David Guzik (Pentecostal/charismatic) notes that the persecution here is "persecution through neglect" — nobody cared when they perished. Yet God used even their suffering to take them away from evil and into peace. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

**Matthew Henry** adds that God removes the righteous partly in compassion (so they do not see the evil, 2 Kings 22:20) and partly in wrath to the world (removing those who stood in the gap to turn away judgment). — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 2 — "Those who walk uprightly enter into peace; they find rest, lying down in death."

**Traditional Reading:** The righteous do not merely "perish" — they *enter into peace*. This is more than just escape from trouble; it is positive rest. The "beds" refer to the grave, pictured as a place of peaceful sleep from which they will awaken at the resurrection. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Calvin writes that believers in death are like discharged soldiers allowed to enjoy ease. They rest in their beds "because they do not yet enjoy perfect blessedness and glory; but they wait for the last day of the resurrection." He insists this proves souls are immortal: "if souls had no feeling…they could not enjoy peace." — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

Gill explains: the righteous man "goes in peace" now (peace through justifying righteousness and faith in Christ), departs life with serenity, and immediately upon death enters a state of perfect peace — the presence of the God of peace. Bodies rest in the grave as in a bed, souls in the bosom of Abraham, awaiting resurrection. — Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/57.htm

The Pulpit Commentary notes that "whosoever hath walked uprightly" refers to the earthly life, not post-death activity, but the peace they enter is positive, not merely negative — otherwise it would be no consolation. — Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 3 — "But come here, you sons of a sorceress, you offspring of adulterers and prostitutes!"

**Traditional Reading:** After describing the peaceful end of the righteous, the prophet turns abruptly with "But draw near hither" — summoning the wicked idolaters to divine judgment. "Sons of the sorceress" and "seed of the adulterer" challenge their proud claim to be Abraham's children. The nation (Judah) is the sorceress/adulteress; her individual children are summoned. — Pulpit: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/isaiah/57.htm

Calvin says the prophet "breaks out with very great vehemence against the wicked, who did not cease to lead a base and shameful life, and were not moved by the death of believers." He notes the prophets frequently had to beat down Jewish pride in their genealogy, calling them bastards and traitors, not true children of Abraham. — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

Ellicott suggests "sorceress" may refer literally to female soothsayers (cf. Ezekiel 13:17–23), with both figurative and literal applications. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Gill, writing from a Baptist perspective with a strong anti-Roman Catholic polemical bent, applies this to "the children of Jezebel, the witch" — the apostate church of Rome, whose sorceries have deceived all nations. — Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 4 — "Whom are you mocking? At whom do you snarl and stick out your tongue? Are you not children of transgression, offspring of deceit…"

**Traditional Reading:** The wicked mocked the righteous — and in doing so, mocked God Himself. The "wide mouth" and "drawn-out tongue" are gestures of scorn and derision. God's question "Against whom?" implies: Do you realise you're not mocking mere men, but God? — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Calvin writes: "When ye put forth the tongue against God, and mock his word, do ye think that ye have to deal with a mortal man?" Wicked people "do not confess that they are rebels against God, and even complain that they are very unjustly treated. But they must be dragged to the light." — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

Guzik adds the pastoral observation: "This speaks to a common sin of human nature — to see the sins or the problems of others while being blind to our own sins or problems." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

---

### v. 5 — "…who burn with lust among the oaks, under every luxuriant tree, who slaughter your children in the valleys, under the clefts of the rocks?"

**Traditional Reading:** The language is both literal and metaphorical. "Inflaming yourselves" describes the orgiastic, fanatical excitement of pagan fertility rites. The Hebrew word for "oaks" (אלים, *elim*) may also mean "gods," creating an intentional double meaning. Child sacrifice — burning infants alive to Molech — is singled out as the most monstrous expression of their apostasy. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Calvin describes how Satan drives idolaters to "madness and rage": "They who do not hesitate to slay their children, as if on the ground of its being a righteous sacrifice, must be in a state of furious madness." He notes the perverse (κακοζηλία) imitation of Abraham — claiming "If we are Abraham's descendants, we ought not to spare our children." But Abraham acted by God's command, and Isaac was not actually sacrificed; these people slew their children on their own authority. — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

Guzik describes the practice vividly: "Molech was 'worshipped' by heating a metal statue representing the god until it was red hot, then by placing a living infant on the outstretched hands of the statue, while beating drums drowned out the screams of the child until it burned to death." He quotes Trapp: "superstition many times outdoeth true religion." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

---

### v. 6 — "Your portion is among the smooth stones of the valley; indeed, they are your lot…"

**Traditional Reading:** "Smooth stones" refers to water-worn stones in stream beds that were venerated or made into idols (cf. the Phoenician *Baetulia*, likely from *Bethel*). The irony is sharp: Israel's true "portion" and "lot" was Jehovah (Psalm 16:5; Jeremiah 10:16), but they have chosen polished stones instead. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Calvin reads "They, they are thy lot" as God's sarcastic permission: "'I leave to you your inventions…I have nothing to do with traitors and apostates.'" He connects it to Moses' declaration that the Lord Himself is the inheritance of His people (Numbers 18:20). Since the Jews had revolted, God justly tells them to keep their idols. — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

The "Should I relent / receive comfort in these?" is taken by the Pulpit Commentary as a rhetorical question: "Shall I be quiet in spite of all this?" The answer is no. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 7 — "On a high and lofty hill you have made your bed, and there you went up to offer sacrifices."

**Traditional Reading:** Continuing the adultery metaphor, the "bed" represents the idolatrous altar on the high place. The height is significant: like a brazen harlot who has lost all shame, Judah practised her idolatry openly, on conspicuous heights, without concealment. — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown commentary notes: "The 'bed' answers to the idolatrous altar, the scene of their spiritual unfaithfulness to their divine husband (Ezekiel 16:16, 25; 23:41)." — JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 8 — "Behind the door and doorpost you have set up your memorial…"

**Traditional Reading:** A perverse inversion of Deuteronomy 6:9, where God commanded Israel to write His words on doorposts. Instead, they set up idolatrous memorials ("remembrance") in that very place. Some commentators suggest the *mezuzah* (scripture scroll) had been deliberately hidden behind the door out of shame over their true creed, while idolatrous symbols took its place on display. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Guzik calls it a "perverse twisting": "The sensitive Israelite reader would, of course, remember that it was the word of God…that was to be inscribed on the doors." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

Calvin reads the "enlarged bed" and "covenant with them" as Judah making room for more and more idols, entering formal covenants with pagan nations and their gods, just as an unfaithful wife makes her bed available to many lovers. — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

---

### v. 9 — "You went to Molech with oil and multiplied your perfumes…"

**Traditional Reading:** Ellicott notes that altering one Hebrew letter would read "to Molech" rather than "to the king." But keeping "the king," he sees it as referring to the great king of Assyria, whose religion and alliances Judah basely courted — just as Ahaz had done (2 Kings 16:11), reproduced by Manasseh. The "ointment" and "perfumes" picture a harlot adorning herself, paralleling Proverbs 7:14–17. Sending "envoys far off" points to the long, costly embassies to Assyria and Babylon. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Guzik interprets "descended even to Sheol" as the depths of degradation to which idolatry drags its devotees. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

---

### v. 10 — "You are wearied by your many journeys, but you did not say, 'There is no hope!'…"

**Traditional Reading:** Despite the exhausting, fruitless pursuit of idols and foreign alliances, Judah refused to admit defeat. The phrase "you found renewal of your strength" (or "life of your hand") means they found a fancied new energy or temporary advantage in their idolatrous diplomacy, so they were not grieved and did not repent. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Guzik observes: "After the initial thrill of their spiritual adultery wore off, they were wearied. But even then, they would not repent." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

Gill, reading with his anti-Roman polemic, sees Rome's tireless pursuit of power: "though the cause was very bad, yet when schemes did not take…no cost nor pains were spared to gain the point in view…through great fatigue and labour, they attained unto" universal empire. — Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 11 — "Whom have you dreaded and feared, so that you lied and failed to remember Me…?"

**Traditional Reading:** God asks why His people fear everything *except* Him. They feared human powers (Assyria, Babylon) and so "lied" — their diplomacy and idolatry were an "acted lie." They mistook God's long silence (His forbearance in not punishing immediately) for weakness or indifference, and therefore did not fear Him. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Guzik: "They made a crucial error, common to fallen humanity: they mistook God's mercy and forbearance for weakness or lack of resolve." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

Matthew Henry notes: "Have not I held my peace even of old? … God's silence is an evidence of His patience, but men misinterpret it as evidence of His indifference." — Matthew Henry (CCEL): https://ccel.org/ccel/henry/mhcc/mhcc.xxiv.lvii.html

---

### v. 12 — "I will expose your righteousness and your works, and they will not profit you."

**Traditional Reading:** God declares He will publicly expose their "righteousness" — used ironically for self-righteousness that is no righteousness at all (cf. Isaiah 64:6). Their works, including their idolatrous "good works," will prove worthless to save them. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

JFB expands: "I will expose publicly thy (hypocritical) righteousness. I will show openly how vain thy works, in having recourse to idols, or foreign alliances, shall prove." — JFB: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 13 — "When you cry out, let your companies of idols deliver you! … But he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land…"

**Traditional Reading:** Sarcastic dare: let the crowd of collected gods ("companies" — a contemptuous term for the multitude of idols Manasseh introduced) save you when trouble comes. The answer: they are so impotent that a mere breath or wind carries them away. Contrast: the one who trusts in Jehovah alone will possess the land and inherit God's holy mountain. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Matthew Henry draws the practical application: "Those that trust in God's providence take the best course to secure their secular interests. They shall possess the land…Those that trust in God's grace take the best course to secure their sacred interests. They shall inherit my holy mountain." — Matthew Henry (Blue Letter Bible): https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Isa/Isa_057.cfm

---

### v. 14 — "And it will be said, 'Build it up, build it up, prepare the way…'"

**Traditional Reading:** A divine voice (literally "one said") renews the cry of Isaiah 40:3 — "prepare the way of the LORD." The command to "build up" or "heap up" refers to constructing a raised highway (cf. Isaiah 35:8), an elevated road above all obstacles, so God's people can return to Him unhindered. "Take every obstacle (stumbling block) out of the way" — whatever blocks our getting right with God must be removed. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Guzik sees this as a transition: after the rebuke of idolatry, God now provides the way back. The "stumbling block" is whatever gets in the way of repentance and restoration. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

---

### v. 15 — "For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy: 'I dwell in a high and holy place, and with the oppressed and humble in spirit…'"

**Traditional Reading:** This is widely regarded as one of the most sublime verses in Isaiah. God is described in His transcendent majesty: He is "high and lifted up" (cf. Isaiah 6:1), "inhabits eternity" (lives forever, beyond time), and His very name is "Holy." Yet this transcendent God also dwells *with* the contrite and lowly — those crushed in spirit. The purpose: to revive the humble and the contrite. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Dr. Constable calls it "one of the finest one-sentence summations of biblical theology in the Bible." — Constable (cited via Precept Austin): https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_commentaries

Calvin would view this through the lens of God's sovereign grace: God, dwelling in inaccessible light, condescends by His own free will to dwell with the humble. This is not because humility merits His presence, but because God's nature is to revive the contrite.

Guzik identifies three requirements for being right with God from this section: (1) understanding His majesty, (2) coming before Him with contrite and humble spirit, and (3) receiving His mercy freely offered. — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

**Lutheran perspective (search result):** The text was referenced by the Precept Austin site in connection with the question "Where Does God Dwell Today?" — noting that God dwells with him "who is contrite and lowly in spirit." This connects with Lutheran emphasis on God's presence among the humble rather than in temples made with hands: https://www.preceptaustin.org/our_body_his_temple

---

### v. 16 — "For I will not accuse you forever, nor will I always be angry…"

**Traditional Reading:** God's anger, though real, has a limit. If He remained angry forever, "the spirit of man would grow weak" — humanity would simply perish. The verse echoes Genesis 6:3 and 8:21 — God's mercy tempers His wrath because He remembers that we are His creatures, the work of His hands. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Matthew Henry: "He will not contend for ever, for he will not forsake the work of his own hands, nor defeat the purchase of his Son's blood." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 17 — "I was enraged by his sinful greed, so I struck him and hid My face in anger; yet he kept turning back to the desires of his heart."

**Traditional Reading:** The specific sin singled out is "covetousness" (or "unjust gain"). This is the root-evil from which other sins sprout (cf. Jeremiah 6:13; 1 Timothy 6:10). God struck Israel in chastisement and hid His face — yet even then, Israel "went on backsliding" (KJV "frowardly in the way of his heart"). Punishment alone did not reform them. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Matthew Henry: "Covetousness is a sin that particularly lays men under the Divine displeasure. See the sinfulness of sin. See also that troubles cannot reform men unless God's grace work in them." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/57.htm

---

### v. 18 — "I have seen his ways, but I will heal him; I will guide him and restore comfort to him and his mourners…"

**Traditional Reading:** Despite having seen their sinful "ways," God promises healing, not destruction. The healing is by grace — God takes the initiative. He will also "lead" (guide) them and restore "comforts" to both the penitent and "his mourners" — those who have grieved over Israel's sin with godly sorrow (2 Corinthians 7:10–11). — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Guzik observes: "The third thing to understand in getting right with God is His great love…Though God disciplined His people, He now says, I have seen his ways, and will heal him." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

---

### v. 19 — "…bringing praise to their lips. Peace, peace to those far and near," says the LORD, "and I will heal them."

**Traditional Reading:** "The fruit of the lips" is praise and thanksgiving — created by God Himself in the pardoned penitent (cf. Hosea 14:2; Hebrews 13:15). The double "Peace, peace" emphasises fullness — perfect peace (shalom). "Far and near" originally meant Jews in exile and Jews in Jerusalem, but Paul in Ephesians 2:17 reveals its fuller meaning: Gentiles (those far off) and Jews (those near) are both brought to peace through Christ. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Guzik: "In Ephesians 2:17, Paul speaks of Jesus fulfilling this promise exactly…Both can come to peace through receiving God's gift through Jesus." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

Matthew Henry adds: "Christ came and preached peace to Gentiles, as well as to the Jews; to after-ages, who were afar off in time, as well as to those of that age." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/57.htm

**Calvin on "far and near":** He notes the Jews were "near" because God had entered into a covenant with them; Gentiles were "far off" as strangers to that covenant — but he says the prophet appears to speak of Jews only (i.e., near = Jerusalem, far = exiles), while the fuller sense is revealed in the New Testament. — https://www.ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom16.x.i.html

---

### v. 20 — "But the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck."

**Traditional Reading:** The sea in ancient Hebrew thought represented chaos, danger, and restlessness. Unlike the calm "peace" of the righteous, the wicked are perpetually agitated — driven by lusts, fears, and the horror of guilt. Just as the sea constantly churns up filth, the wicked produce moral filth from their restless lives. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Ellicott suggests the "sea" may specifically be the Dead Sea, casting up its salt and bituminous deposits. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Guzik notes this is "a good example of how the sea was thought to be a dangerous, dark, restless place in the mind of the ancient Jews. No wonder that in the new heaven and the new earth, there is no more sea (Revelation 21:1)." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

---

### v. 21 — "'There is no peace,' says my God, 'for the wicked.'"

**Traditional Reading:** The chapter ends with the same watchword that closed Isaiah 48:22, marking the close of another major section. The phrase "my God" is striking — the prophet claims God as his own God in a personal way. Ellicott notes that some ancient manuscripts and versions seem uneasy with this boldness, substituting "saith the LORD" or "saith God" — but "my God" is a characteristic touch of Isaiah (cf. Isaiah 7:13). — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

Matthew Henry: "God hath said it, and all the world cannot unsay it, That there is no peace to those who allow themselves in any sin. If we are recovered from such an awful state, it is only by the grace of God." — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/57.htm

Poole (cited by Guzik): "Their minds are restless, being perpetually hurried and tormented with their own lusts and passions, and with the horror of their guilt, and the dread of Divine vengeance due unto them." — Enduring Word: https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Very little doctrinal divergence between traditions emerged from these sources on Isaiah 57 specifically; all surveyed commentators read the passage similarly, seeing it as a rebuke of idolatry and a promise of grace to the humble. The main differences are ones of *emphasis*:

1. **Reformed (Calvin):** Emphasises God's sovereign initiative — the wicked are summoned to God's judgment seat and cannot escape; God "sees" sinful ways and chooses to heal. Dwells on the reprobate's blindness to providence. The peace of the righteous at death is real but incomplete until the resurrection. — Calvin: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/isaiah-57.html

2. **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Guzik / Enduring Word):** Emphasises application — examining our own "idols," the need for contrition, and receiving God's mercy. Highlights the emotional/pastoral dimensions: the weariness of sin, the "initial thrill" of idolatry wearing off. More likely to apply the text directly to contemporary Christian life rather than historical Israel. — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

3. **Older Baptist (Gill):** Reads the idolatry language as directly prophetic of the Roman Catholic Church — "the great whore of Babylon," the pope as antichrist, the mass as a "drink offering" to idols. This strongly polemical reading interprets most details through an anti-papal lens. — Gill: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/57.htm

4. **Anglican (Ellicott):** More historical-critical in orientation — discusses textual variants, Hebrew readings, and the specific historical context (Manasseh's reign, Assyrian alliances). Sees the text against its ancient Near Eastern background. Notes the NT use in Ephesians 2:17. — Ellicott: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/isaiah/57.htm

5. **Puritan/Evangelical (Matthew Henry):** Focuses on practical godliness and the devotional life. Emphasises that "covetousness" draws God's particular displeasure; that "troubles cannot reform men unless God's grace work in them"; and that peace comes from trusting God's providence and grace. — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/isaiah/57.htm

---

## Other Views

**Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I was unable to reach these sources (newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org) within the search/fetch limits available.

**Modern scholarship:** I was unable to reach bibleodyssey.org or netbible.org within the available limits. The Constable Expository Notes (available on StudyLight) and Bible.org were located in search results but could not be fully fetched. However, search excerpts indicate that modern evangelical scholarship (Oswalt, Motyer) confirms the chapter's pre-exilic setting: "There is no evidence of corresponding post-exilic practices. A prophet in the post-exile could not have written like this" (Motyer, cited by Guzik). — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-57/

**Debated popular teachings (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** No specific sources addressing Isaiah 57 from these perspectives were found in the searches. However, the text's promises (inheriting the land, healing, peace) are sometimes cited by prosperity teachers to claim material blessing; the traditional reading uniformly interprets "inherit the land / holy mountain" as spiritual and eschatological inheritance, not material prosperity in this life.
